title: "Ethereal mediator"
author: "Tim Gorringe"

Newton's law of gravity and Coulomb's law of electricity leave an obvious
question unanswered. "How do two masses or two charges that are spatially
separated exert forces on one another?" This puzzle is called
action-at-a-distance and maybe is particularly unsettling when you remember that
pushing or pulling an object involves touching the object. By what mechanism
does one charge influence another charge or one mass influence another mass
through empty space?

The action-at-a-distance puzzle was solved by Michael Faraday. Faraday was
influential, nineteenth century, English scientist with transformational
contributions in physics and chemistry. In particular he introduced the notion
of fields into science. It's an electric field that conveys the electric force
between two charges across empty space between and it's a gravitational field
that conveys the gravitational force between two masses across empty space.
Specifically, the electric force acting on a charge arises from its immersion in
the electric fields of other charges. And the gravitational force acting on a
mass arises from its immersion in the gravitational fields of other masses.

The electric field is a physical, immaterial, continuous medium that surrounds
every charge and fills all space. By physical, I mean it's a real entity, and by
immaterial, I mean it's not a material substance. And by continuous, I mean it's
smoothly varying across space.

Importantly, the electric field is a vector field with a magnitude and a
direction. The field exists at every point in the universe and associated with
each point in space is a vector **E**(r). At some level - through the fabric of
the field - every charge in the universe interacts with every other charge in
the universe.

The electric field E of a point charge q is given by E = kq/r^2^ (where r is the
distance from the field-point to the charge). For a positive charge the field
direction is radially outwards. For a negative charge the field direction is
radially inwards. Note, as the magnitude of the field falls-off with the
inverse-square distance, the field is much stronger near to the charge, and much
weaker far from the charge. And note, as the magnitude of the field is in
proportion to the magnitude of the charge, a large charge supports a
correspondingly large field, and a small charge supports a correspondingly small
field. Every charged particle (electron, proton, etc.) in the universe is a
source of an electric field.

The electric force F on a point charge q is given by F = q E (where E is the
field at the location of the charge). According to F = q E a large charge q
feels a larger force and a small charge q feels a smaller force in the same
electric field E. Note that if the charge is positive the force is in the same
direction as the field, whereas, if the charge is negative the force is in the
opposite direction to the electric field.

By combining the point charge field E = kq/r^2^ and field equation F = q E we
can evaluate the resulting force between two point charges q~1~, q~2~ with
separation r. The force F~1-\>2~ on q~2~ due to q~1~ is a result of the field
E~1~ of the charge q~1~ at the location of the charge q~2~. The argument gives
F~1-\>2~ = q~2~ E~1~ = k q~1~ q~2~ / r^2^ and reproduces Coulomb's law.
Likewise, the force F~2-\>1~ on q~1~ due to q~2~ is a result of the field E~2~
of the q~2~ at the location of the charge q~1~. The argument gives F~2-\>1~ =
q~1~ E~2~ = k q~1~ q~2~ / r^2^ and again reproduces Coulomb's law. Furthermore,
the combination of the radially inwards / outwards fields of negative / positive
charges, and the relative directions of the fields / forces in the field
equation, yields the experimental fact that like-charges repel and
unlike-charges attract.

You might be unsettled by the following issue. Charge q~1~ experiences the field
of charge q~2~ but doesn't experience its own field. And charge q~2~ experiences
the field of charge q~1~ but doesn't experience its own field. Why are charges
blind to their 'self-field' or 'self-interaction'?

One answer I'll offer is point-charge electric fields are spherically symmetric.
A point charge field doesn't discriminate up from down, left from right, and so
on. The point-charge field is identical or indistinguishable in every
orientation. Therefore, a self-force from a self-interaction couldn't act
upwards or downwards down or any other direction. (Maybe a self-force could act
to explode a point charge but exploding a single point isn't really intelligible
either).

A fuller answer is found by considering the quantum electric fields and
sub-atomic particles, e.g., electrons, protons. An electron does self-interact
with its own electric field. And a proton does self-interact with its own
electric field. When we measure the properties of sub-atomic particles there
properties often incorporate this self-interaction (a very famous example of its
self-interaction is the electron's magnetism).

The concept of fields as mediators of forces was a monumental breakthrough in
science and is the framework or the template for the working of all the forces
of nature. From this mechanism, the superposition of electric forces arising
from individual charges is seen to emerge from the superposition of electric
fields arising from individual charges.

To help us visualize these fields we'll detour this physics class into an art
class and learn to draw the electric fields of charge distributions. Through the
use of lines of field we'll denote strong fields by tightly-packed lines, weak
fields by loosely-packed field lines, and the direction of the field by the
direction of the lines. These sketches of field lines of charge distributions
offer an intuitive, visceral sense of the otherwise abstract, electric fields
(and show there's art in science).

An electric dipole is an assembly of equal-sized, opposite-signed charges q with
separation d. The H~2~O mole is a famous example of an electric dipole - its
positive-end being the hydrogen ions and its negative-end being the oxygen ion.
The fact the H~2~O molecules are dipoles is why H~2~O is a liquid at room
temperatures, a solvent of hydrophilic ("water-loving") molecules, and 60% of
human bodies. Using the superposition principle we'll both calculate and sketch
the electric field surround the water molecule and other electric dipoles.
